SOURCE ESSAY:
My hostess and her daughter met me at the station in the little pony-cart and we set off at a gentle trot, conversing as we went. That is to say, they asked questions about London and the great wicked world, and I endeavoured to answer them.

It was high if premature summer; the sky was blue, the hedges and the grass were growing almost audibly, the birds sang, the sun blazed, and, to lighten the burden, I walked up two or three hills without the faintest enthusiasm.

Just after the top of the last hill, when I had again resumed my seat (at the risk once more of lifting the pony into the zenith), the ladies simultaneously uttered a shrill cry of dismay.

"Look!" they exclaimed; "there's Bunty!"

I looked, and beheld in the road before us a small West Highland terrier, as white as a recent ratting foray in a wet ditch would allow.

"Bunty! Bunty! you wicked dog!" they cried; "how dare you go hunting?"

To this question Bunty made no other reply than to subside under the hedge, where a little shade was to be had, in an attitude of exhaustion tempered by wariness.

"How very naughty!" said my hostess. "I left her in the house."

"Yes," said the daughter, "and if she's going to go off hunting like this what on earth shall we do? There'll be complaints from every one. She's never done it before."

"Come, Bunty!" said my hostess, in the wheedling tones of dog-owners whose dogs notoriously obey their slightest word. But Bunty sat tight.

"If we drive on perhaps she'll follow," said the daughter, and we drove on a few yards; but Bunty did not move.

We stopped again, while coaxing noises were made, calculated to soften the hearts of rocks; but Bunty refused to stir.

"She'll come on later," I suggested.

"Oh, no," said her elderly mistress, "we couldn't risk leaving her here, when she's never gone off alone before. Bunty! Bunty! don't be so naughty. Come along, there's a dear little Bunty."

But Bunty merely glittered at us through her white-hair entanglement and remained perfectly still.

Strange dogs are not much in my line; but since my hostess was no longer very active, and the daughter was driving, and no one else was present, there seemed to be a certain inevitableness about the proposition which I then made that I should get out and bring the miscreant in.

"Oh, would you mind?" my hostess said. "She won't bite, I promise you. She's a perfect dear."

Trying hard to forget how painful to legs or hands can be the smart closing of the snappy jaws of dogs that won't bite, I advanced stealthily towards Bunty, murmuring ingratiating words.

When I was quite close she turned over on her back, lifted her paws, and obviously commended her soul to Heaven; and I had therefore no difficulty in lifting her up and carrying her to the trap.

Her mistresses received her with rapture, disguised, but by no means successfully, by reproach and reproof, and we were beginning to drive on again when an excited voice called upon us to stop, and a strange lady, of the formidable unmarried kind, with a very red face beneath a purple parasol, confronted us.

"What," she panted, "is the meaning of this outrage? How dare you steal my dog?"

"Your dog, madam?" I began.

"It's no use denying it," she burst in, "I saw you do it. I saw you pick it up and carry it to the trap. It's—it's monstrous. I shall go to the police about it."

Meanwhile, it cannot be denied, the dog was showing signs of delight and recognition such as had previously been lacking.

"But——" began my hostess, who is anything but quarrelsome.

"We ought to know our own dog when we see it," said the daughter, who does not disdain a fight.

"Certainly," said the angry lady, "if you have a dog of your own."

"Of course we have," said the daughter; "we have a West Highland named Bunty."

"This happens to be my West Highland, named Wendy," said the lady, "as you will see if you look on the collar. My name is there too—Miss Morrison, 14 Park Terrace, W. I am staying at Well House Farm."

And it was so.

It was on the tip of my tongue to point out that collars, being easily exchangeable, are not evidence; but I thought it better that any such suggestion should come from elsewhere.

"It is certainly very curious," said the daughter, submitting the features of the dog to the minutest scrutiny; "if it is not Bunty it is her absolute double."

"It is not Bunty, but Wendy," said Miss Morrison coldly; "and I shall be glad if you will give her to me."

"But——" the daughter began.

"Yes, give the lady the dog," said the mother.

In the regrettable absence of Solomon, who would, of course, have cut the little devil in two, there was nothing for it but to surrender; and the couple went off together, the dog exhibiting every sign of pleasure.

Meanwhile the daughter whipped up the pony, and we soon entered the gates.

In the drive, awaiting us, was a West Highland terrier named Bunty.

"There!" cried the ladies, as they scrambled out and flung themselves on her.

"Of course she's not a bit like that Wendy thing really," said the mother.

"Now that I come to look at her I can see heaps of difference," said the daughter.

"None the less," I interjected, "you turned a very honest man into a thief, and a dog-thief at that; and he insists on reparation."

"Yes, indeed," said the mother, "it is really too bad. What reparation can we make?"

I don't pretend that my feelings are completely soothed, but the Clicquot 1904 which took the place of claret at dinner that evening was certainly very good.

Upon my arrival at the station, my hostess and her daughter greeted me with a pony-cart, and we set off at a leisurely pace, engaging in conversation. They posed numerous questions about London and the so-called wicked world, and I did my best to respond.

It was a season of early summer, bright and vibrant; the sky was a clear blue, the grass and hedges seemed to grow audibly, the birds filled the air with their melodies, and the sun shone brilliantly. To ease the journey, I ascended a couple of hills, though I felt little enthusiasm for the exertion.

Just after reaching the summit of the last hill, I settled back into my seat, which risked lifting the pony off the ground, when suddenly, both ladies emitted a sharp cry of alarm.

"Look!" they exclaimed in unison. "There’s Bunty!"

I turned my gaze to find a small West Highland terrier in the road, her coat as white as a freshly washed rag after a dip in a muddy ditch.

"Bunty! You naughty dog!" they scolded. "How could you go off hunting?"

In response to their reprimand, Bunty simply ducked under a nearby hedge, seeking a sliver of shade, appearing both exhausted and cautious.

"My goodness, how naughty she is!" my hostess lamented. "I left her inside the house."

"Yes," her daughter added, "if she’s going to go hunting like this, we’ll have complaints from everyone. She has never done this before."

"C’mon, Bunty!" my hostess called in the sweet tones of a dog owner who believes their pet will respond to any entreaty. But Bunty remained motionless.

"Perhaps if we drive a little further, she’ll follow us," suggested the daughter, and we moved forward a few yards, but Bunty did not budge.

We halted again, making coaxing sounds that might soften the resolve of stone, yet Bunty remained steadfast in her refusal to move.

"I think she’ll come along eventually," I proposed.

"Oh no," her elderly mistress replied, "we can’t leave her here when she has never wandered off alone before. Bunty! Bunty! Don’t be such a naughty girl. Come on, dear little Bunty."

Yet Bunty simply stared at us through her tangled fur, remaining utterly still.

I wasn't particularly fond of strange dogs, but with my hostess unable to move quickly and her daughter at the reins, it felt inevitable that I would need to intervene and retrieve the misbehaving terrier.

"Would you mind?" my hostess asked. "I assure you, she won’t bite. She’s a sweetheart."

Forcing myself to forget the potential pain inflicted by the snap of a dog's jaws, I crept toward Bunty, murmuring soft words in an attempt to win her over.

As I approached, she flopped over onto her back, raised her paws in surrender, and appeared to plead for mercy. I had no trouble picking her up and carrying her back to the cart.

Her mistresses welcomed her back with enthusiasm, masked by the pretense of reproach, and we were about to continue on our way when an agitated voice called out for us to stop. A formidable-looking woman, with a very red face and a purple parasol, confronted us.

"What," she panted, "is the meaning of this? How dare you take my dog?"

"Your dog, madam?" I began to explain.

"It’s useless to deny it," she interjected. "I saw you pick her up and carry her to the trap. This is outrageous. I will report you to the police."

At that moment, I had to admit, the dog was displaying signs of delight and recognition that had been absent before.

"But—" my hostess started, not one for conflict.

"We ought to recognize our own dog when we see her," the daughter chimed in, not shying away from a confrontation.

"Certainly," replied the furious woman, "if you actually have a dog of your own."

"Of course we do," the daughter asserted. "We have a West Highland terrier named Bunty."

"This is my West Highland, named Wendy," the woman declared coldly, "as you can see by the collar. My name is also on there—Miss Morrison, 14 Park Terrace, W. I’m staying at Well House Farm."

And indeed, it was true.

I was on the verge of pointing out that collars can be swapped easily and thus are not definitive proof of ownership, but I thought it wise to let that suggestion arise from elsewhere.

"It’s quite curious," the daughter remarked, scrutinizing the dog closely. "If this isn’t Bunty, it’s her exact double."

"It is not Bunty, but Wendy," Miss Morrison replied frostily. "I would appreciate it if you would return her to me."

"But—" the daughter began again.

"Yes, please return the dog to the lady," the mother intervened.

In the unfortunate absence of Solomon, who would have surely divided the little creature in two, we had no choice but to comply, and the two departed, the dog clearly delighted in the company.

Meanwhile, the daughter urged the pony forward, and we soon passed through the gates.

Awaiting us in the driveway was a West Highland terrier named Bunty.

"There!" the ladies exclaimed as they jumped out and rushed toward her.

"Of course, she doesn’t resemble that Wendy creature at all," the mother noted.

"Now that I take a closer look, I can see numerous differences," the daughter added.

"Nevertheless," I interjected, "you’ve transformed an honest man into a thief—a dog thief, no less—and I demand compensation."

"Indeed," the mother replied, "this is truly unacceptable. What reparation can we offer?"

Although my feelings were not entirely assuaged, the fine Clicquot 1904 that replaced claret at dinner that evening was certainly enjoyable.
